\chapter{Synthesis --- Two Shores, Two Answers}
\label{ch:synthesis-perfect}
\hlchaptermodality{104}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what the perfect does that the preterite does not, and that today takes different tenses in Spain and Latin America.}

Complete ES-C49-sintesis-dos-orillas: contrast he comido with comi, and say which tense Madrid and Mexico City choose for today.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — two shores, two answers}

\label{lesson:ES-C49-sintesis-dos-orillas}



\begin{quote}
You can now say \textquotedblleft{}I spoke\textquotedblright{} two ways: \emph{hablé} and \emph{he hablado}. The obvious question is which one to use, and it has an unusual answer.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the perfect is for}]
Start with the part everybody agrees on. The perfect reaches into \textbf{now}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{He comido.} — I have eaten. \emph{(so I am not hungry)} \emph{Comí.} — I ate. \emph{(a finished event, back there)}
\end{quote}

The preterite puts an event in the past and leaves it there. The perfect drags it forward and makes it matter now — the tense is telling your listener what to do with the information, not when it happened. English agrees: \emph{I have eaten} and \emph{I ate} are not interchangeable for you either.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Now the part nobody agrees on, and it is worth having straight before you are corrected by two people who contradict each other.

For something that happened \textbf{today}, Spain and most of Latin America choose differently:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Hoy \textbf{he hablado} con Ana.} — \textbf{Spain.} \emph{Hoy \textbf{hablé} con Ana.} — \textbf{most of Latin America.}
\end{quote}

Same day, same conversation, both entirely correct. Spain uses the perfect for anything inside the current stretch of time; much of Latin America uses the preterite and saves the perfect for things whose relevance is still open.

Third split in this book decided by \textbf{geography rather than meaning}, after \emph{vosotros} and \emph{os}. There is no version of Spanish that is the real one, and no choice here that will make you wrong.

A default, if you want one: the Latin American pattern is understood everywhere and is what most learners meet first, so leaning on the preterite for finished events is a safe habit. In Spain you will hear the perfect constantly and pick it up in a week.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}He comido\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Comí\textquotedblright{} — one reaches into now, one does not
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Hoy he hablado con Ana\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Hoy hablé con Ana\textquotedblright{} — two shores
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the perfect do that the preterite does not? (\textbf{Reaches into now.}) And for something that happened today? (\textbf{Spain} says \emph{he hablado}; \textbf{much of Latin America} says \emph{hablé} — and both are right.)
\end{tcolorbox}
